paragraphs.text: [Ya Shi Xiang](dancong:ya-shi-xiang), duck dung in its Chinese name, is the market name for one line of Dancong, traced to Pingkengtou village. Most lists of the ten classic kinds leave it out, though it sells widely. In 2014 a second name, Yinhua Xiang, silver flower, was put forward, and many sellers keep the old one. Three stories explain the name, all told as stories: that it was chosen to put thieves off the bush, that it comes from the yellow local soil called duck dung soil, and that duck droppings lay on the bush.

The leaf grows on [Phoenix Mountain](phoenix-mountain:where-it-is), the range in Chaozhou in eastern Guangdong, where gardens climb from low foothills to roughly 1,100 metres. Cloud and [mist](phoenix-mountain:mist-and-climate) sit on the upper slopes for much of the year and the nights are cool, so the bushes grow slowly. [Dancong](dancong:name) means single bush, the leaf of one bush made on its own, though today a named line is mostly grown from cuttings or grafts, so one name no longer means one tree. As an [oolong](oolong:definition), it is partly oxidised, between green tea and red.

brewing.text: Brew it gongfu style in a small gaiwan or clay pot, with about 3 to 8 grams for 100 to 120 ml and hot water, about 88 to 100°C; Chinese accounts mostly say 95 to 100°C. A quick rinse is common. Steeps start at a few seconds and grow a few seconds each round, and a good Dancong gives about eight to fifteen. Too long, too hot or too much leaf and it turns bitter and astringent.

notice.text: Flowers above all, a sweetness that comes back after swallowing, a high scent that lasts, honey, often ripe fruit such as peach, and what the trade calls mountain rhyme, shan yun; a liquor from golden to orange-red or amber.
